name: The Bandwagon Effect
statement: The more people adopt something, the more others adopt it, just because others have.
meaning: The bandwagon effect is the tendency to adopt beliefs, behaviours, or purchases in proportion to how many others have already done so. The rate of uptake rises the more people have taken something up, producing a self-reinforcing loop, captured in the phrase jumping on the bandwagon. It is a form of herd behaviour and social proof, in which the popularity of a choice becomes a reason to make it, somewhat apart from its own merits.
mechanism: Several drivers feed the loop. A desire to conform and to gain approval pulls people toward what others do, and informational social influence leads us to treat others' choices as evidence of what is good or correct. Fear of missing out and attraction to the winning side add momentum, and in some cases genuine network effects mean a choice really does become more valuable as more adopt it. Because each adoption raises the visible popularity that draws the next, the process compounds.

examples.text: Styles spread as their growing popularity itself becomes the reason more people take them up, catalysed by visible early adopters.
Rising candidates attract further support, and polls showing a frontrunner can sway voters and resources toward the apparent winner.
In markets and on social media, buying or joining because others are doing so can inflate asset bubbles and drive viral adoption.

variants.name: The snob effect
variants.text: Leibenstein's opposite case, in which demand for a good falls as more people adopt it, so exclusivity rather than popularity drives desire.

variants.name: Network effects
variants.text: The distinct case where a good genuinely gains value as more people use it, which can coincide with but differs from purely social bandwagon adoption.

whyItMatters: It shapes consumer demand, voting and polling behaviour, marketing, and finance, where it helps inflate bubbles, and it is central to the diffusion of innovations. By showing how popularity can propagate a choice with little regard to its merits, it warns against mistaking widespread adoption for evidence of value, and it informs both those who would ride a trend and those who would resist one.

working.text: ask whether a choice is good on its own terms or merely widely adopted, since uptake can spread with little supporting evidence.
check whether more adopters genuinely add value, a network effect, or only add social pressure to conform.
notice the attraction to apparent winners in polls and markets, which can amplify a trend beyond its fundamentals.

limits: It is well documented as a real social phenomenon, but its strength varies by context, so it is better treated as a robust tendency than a fixed law. It is the opposite of the snob effect and is distinct from genuine network effects, where a good truly gains value with adoption; the two can coexist but differ. Leibenstein formalised the economic version, but the political and etymological history, including the Dan Rice and Zachary Taylor anecdote, is traditional and semi-legendary in its specifics.
misreadings: It is not the same as a network effect, which reflects real added value from more users rather than a social cue. It is not the Veblen effect, which is driven by high price signalling prestige rather than by the number of others adopting. Leibenstein did not invent the term, which is a nineteenth-century American political and circus coinage; he formalised the economic concept in 1950.
origin: The phrase comes from mid-nineteenth-century American politics and circus parades; the economic concept was formalised by Harvey Leibenstein in his 1950 Quarterly Journal of Economics paper on bandwagon, snob, and Veblen effects.

sources.text: Leibenstein, "Bandwagon, Snob, and Veblen Effects in the Theory of Consumers' Demand," Quarterly Journal of Economics 64 (1950): 183-207. — the economic formalisation and the contrast with snob and Veblen effects.
